title: Celibacy and the Single Life
lead: Most of the Bible assumes marriage and children as the normal path, but it also honors those who do not marry: Jeremiah, forbidden to marry as a sign (Jeremiah 16:1–4), the faithful eunuchs of Isaiah 56, Jesus' "eunuchs for the kingdom" (Matthew 19:12), and Paul's gift of singleness (1 Corinthians 7). Churches differ on whether celibacy is a higher calling and whether clergy may be required to keep it.

sections.b: Jewish teaching treated marriage and children as a duty: the Mishnah rules that a man may not stop trying to have children until he has at least a son and a daughter (Mishnah Yevamot 6:6). A few voices stood apart. The sage Ben Azzai never married, and when challenged said, "My soul longs for the Torah; the world can be kept going by others" (Babylonian Talmud, Yevamot 63b). Ancient writers describe Essenes who did not marry: Josephus says they disdained marriage, though one branch of them married (Jewish War 2.120–121, 160–161), Philo says they avoided it (Hypothetica 11.14), and Pliny the Elder describes a community by the Dead Sea living "without women" (Natural History 5.73). So Jesus' saying about "eunuchs for the kingdom" spoke into a world where staying single was unusual but not unknown.

Genesis gives the blessing "be fruitful and multiply" (Genesis 1:28), and childlessness was a grief in Israel. Yet the prophets already widen the picture: Jeremiah stays unmarried as a sign of coming disaster (Jeremiah 16:1–4), and Isaiah promises eunuchs who keep the covenant "a name that is better than sons and daughters" (Isaiah 56:3–5). Jesus, unmarried himself, speaks of those who "made themselves eunuchs because of the kingdom of heaven" (Matthew 19:12), and Paul, also unmarried, calls singleness and marriage each a gift (1 Corinthians 7:7, 32–35). Revelation pictures the 144,000 as virgins (Revelation 14:4).
